paraphrase: Chapter III opens. Concentration (samādhi) was named, under the heading of consciousness (citta), in the verse "established in virtue, a wise man develops consciousness and understanding"; so it is to be developed. But stated so briefly it is hard even to understand, let alone develop. To show its detail and the method of developing it, eight questions are set: what is concentration; in what sense is it so called; what are its mark, function, manifestation and proximate cause; how many kinds; what is its defilement; what is its cleansing; how is it developed; what is the benefit of developing it.
speaker: Buddhaghosa (author of the commentary; quotations from the discourses are marked as such)
translation_basis: own paraphrase made directly from the Pali (IAST) text of the PTS edition; no published translation consulted

fidelity.note: Individually read by J against the Pali of the page (the fixed-seed 10% sample was below 95%, so every entry was checked). Faithful as written.

notes: Chapter opening; these eight questions are the plan of the whole treatment of concentration (Vism III-XI).

Concentration is of many kinds, and to set out all of them would not serve the purpose and would only lead to distraction; so only the kind meant here is stated: wholesome one-pointedness of consciousness (kusalacittekaggatā) is concentration. paraphrase: Concentration is that state by whose power consciousness and its concomitants remain evenly and rightly on one object, undistracted and unscattered. Its mark (lakkhaṇa) is non-distraction; its function (rasa) is to eliminate distraction; its manifestation (paccupaṭṭhāna) is non-wavering; and, since "the mind of one who is happy is concentrated", its proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna) is happiness (sukha).
speaker: Buddhaghosa (author of the commentary; quotations from the discourses are marked as such)

paraphrase: Fourth question, how many kinds. By its mark concentration is one. By access and absorption (upacāra, appanā) it is two; likewise by worldly and supramundane, with rapture and without rapture, accompanied by happiness and by equanimity. It is three by inferior, middling and superior, and likewise by with/without applied and sustained thought, accompanied by rapture, and limited/exalted/measureless. It is four by painful or pleasant practice with slow or quick direct-knowledge, and in other ways; five by the five jhāna factors in the fivefold reckoning.

paraphrase: Explaining the twofold division. Access concentration (upacāra-samādhi) is the one-pointedness obtained by way of the six grounds of recollection, mindfulness of death, the recollection of peace, the perception of repulsiveness in nutriment and the defining of the four elements, together with the one-pointedness in the stage preceding the absorption concentrations. Because of the saying "the preparation for the first jhāna is a condition, as proximity condition, for the first jhāna", the one-pointedness that immediately follows the preparation is absorption concentration (appanā-samādhi). Thus concentration is twofold as access and absorption.
speaker: Buddhaghosa (author of the commentary; quotations from the discourses are marked as such)

paraphrase: Continuing the kinds. With and without rapture: in the fourfold reckoning the one-pointedness in the first two jhānas, and in the fivefold reckoning in the first three, is with rapture; in the remaining two jhānas it is without rapture; access concentration may be either. Accompanied by happiness or by equanimity: in the fourfold reckoning the one-pointedness in three jhānas, and in the fivefold in four, is accompanied by happiness, in the remaining one by equanimity; access may be either. Threefold: merely obtained is inferior, not very well developed is middling, well developed and mastered is superior. With applied and sustained thought (the first-jhāna concentration together with access); with sustained thought only (the second jhāna in the fivefold reckoning, reached by one who sees danger only in applied thought and seeks only its abandoning); without either (the one-pointedness in the second and later jhānas in the fourfold, the third and later in the fivefold reckoning). Accompanied by rapture (in the first two jhānas of the fourfold and the first three of the fivefold reckoning), by happiness (in the third and fourth), by equanimity (in the last); access may be accompanied by rapture and happiness or by equanimity. Limited (one-pointedness in the plane of access), exalted (in wholesome fine-material and immaterial consciousness), measureless (associated with the noble path).

paraphrase: Fourfold. Concentration may be by painful practice with slow direct-knowledge, painful practice with quick direct-knowledge, pleasant practice with slow, or pleasant practice with quick. From the first attention up to the access of a given jhāna, the development of concentration is called the practice (paṭipadā); from access up to absorption the understanding is called direct-knowledge (abhiññā). The practice is painful for one for whom the hindrances and other opposed states arise and are hard to overcome; it is pleasant for one for whom they do not.

paraphrase: What makes practice painful or pleasant, direct-knowledge slow or quick. One who uses what is unsuitable (asappāya) has painful practice and slow direct-knowledge; one who uses what is suitable has pleasant practice and quick direct-knowledge; mixed use gives mixed results. One who has not cut the impediments and done the preliminary work has painful practice; one who has not perfected the skills in absorption has slow direct-knowledge. The division may also be seen by craving and ignorance (craving-overpowered: painful; ignorance-overpowered: slow), by earlier work in calm and in insight, and by strong or weak defilements and sharp or dull faculties.

paraphrase: Limited and measureless. Concentration that is not well practised and cannot be a condition for a higher jhāna is limited (paritta); one occurring on an object not enlarged is "with a limited object"; concentration well practised, well developed and able to be a condition for a higher jhāna is measureless (appamāṇa), and one occurring on an enlarged object has a measureless object; the mixed cases are understood by combining these marks. Then fourfold by the jhāna factors: the first jhāna has five factors (applied thought, sustained thought, rapture, happiness, concentration) once the hindrances are suppressed; the second has three (applied and sustained thought stilled); the third two (rapture faded away); the fourth two, by way of concentration accompanied by equanimous feeling, with happiness abandoned. The four concentrations that are factors of these four jhānas make four.
speaker: Buddhaghosa (author of the commentary; quotations from the discourses are marked as such)

paraphrase: Seventh question, how concentration is to be developed. The supramundane concentration associated with the noble path is developed by the method of developing understanding, so nothing separate is said. paraphrase: A story of two clansmen who left Anurādhapura and went forth at Thūpārāma. One, having learned two summaries (mātikā) and kept five rains, went to the eastern district; after long residence there he became an elder and, thinking the place fit for seclusion, went back to invite his friend. The friend, greeting him, looked after him in the proper way. The visitor, on the first night, expected gifts of ghee, sugar-syrup or a drink, and then breakfast; getting none, and after a poor alms round, asked whether the elder always lived like this; on being told yes, he said the eastern district was pleasant and they should go there; the elder left the town by the south gate.

paraphrase: Continuing the Koraṇḍaka story: the young monk arrived at the monastery on the day the rains-residence began and took the lodging his father had built. His father, hearing that a young visiting monk had it, came and asked whether there was a duty toward a resident in his lodging (eating in his house for three months); the monk stayed silent. The parents' family did not recognise him and he took his alms there for the whole three months without making himself known; at the end, given oil, a lump of sugar and cloth, he left. He met his preceptor on the road and gave him oil for his feet, sugar for a drink, and the cloth, saying Rohaṇa was suited to him. When the preceptor reached Koraṇḍaka the mother, seeing him alone, wept, thinking her son was dead, and the elder told her that the young monk, of few wishes, had not made himself known.

paraphrase: The story ends: the elder consoled her, told her everything and showed the cloth from his bowl-bag. The mother, gladdened, lay face down toward the direction her son had gone and, paying homage, said that the Blessed One must have taught the Rathavinīta practice, the Nālaka practice, the Tuvaṭaka practice and the great Noble-lineage practice, which show contentment with the four requisites and delight in development, taking a monk like her son as a body-witness; she marvelled that one who ate for three months in the house of the mother who bore him never said "I am the son, you are the mother". Even the parents of such a monk are not impediments, much less another family of supporters.

paraphrase: The Cūḷābhaya story ends. Sent by his preceptor to the elder Mahā-Dhammarakkhita at Tulādhārapabbata, Abhaya recited the scriptures to him by night and the elder expounded them by day. When the exposition was finished, the elder sat on a mat before Abhaya and asked him for a meditation subject; Abhaya, then a stream-enterer, protested that he had heard it all from the elder himself; the elder answered: "the path of one who has gone there is a different thing." Abhaya gave him the subject and left; later, while expounding the Dhamma at the Lohapāsāda, he heard that the elder had attained final nibbāna, and said that the arahat path was fitting for his teacher, an upright thoroughbred who had sat on a mat before his own Dhamma-pupil to ask for a subject. For such as these, study is not an impediment.

paraphrase: Turning to "having approached a good friend who gives a meditation subject": a meditation subject is of two kinds, the universal (sabbatthaka) and the special (pārihāriya). The universal subject is loving-kindness toward the monks and so on, and mindfulness of death, and, some say, the perception of foulness. The meditation-subject practiser first delimits the community of monks within the boundary and develops loving-kindness toward them ("may they be happy, free from hate"), then the deities of the boundary, then the influential people of the alms-village, then the people there, then all beings.

paraphrase: Reasons the universal subject is called universal. Loving-kindness toward the monks makes co-residents gentle-minded; toward the deities of the boundary it brings their righteous protection; toward the influential people of the village it brings well-guarded requisites; toward the people it brings freedom from contempt; toward all beings it lets one go about unobstructed anywhere. Mindfulness of death, thinking "I must die", makes one give up wrong seeking and grow in urgency and unsluggish living. For one whose mind is used to the perception of foulness even divine objects do not overpower the mind through greed. Being so helpful and to be desired everywhere, they are the "universal subject" and the ground of the yoga-work.

paraphrase: How to choose the giver of the subject. Even a taint-destroyer (khīṇāsava) is told to declare himself only when he knows the pupil is a doer of the subject (the story of Assaguttatthera, who sat cross-legged on a piece of hide in the air to teach). If no taint-destroyer is available, the subject is taken from a non-returner, once-returner, stream-enterer, one with jhāna (a worldling), or a holder of three, two or one Piṭaka, taking the earlier in that order; if there is not even a one-Piṭaka holder, from one who has one recitation with its commentary well in hand and is himself conscientious (lajjī), who is a keeper of the tradition and holds the teachers' view, not his own. The taint-destroyers and the like teach only the way they themselves reached; the learned, having approached different teachers, will teach the subject showing the great road as a great elephant does. So one approaches such a person and performs the duties toward him before taking the subject.
speaker: Buddhaghosa (author of the commentary; quotations from the discourses are marked as such)

paraphrase: If the giver is in the same monastery, well; if not, one goes where he lives. One should not set out with feet washed and anointed, wearing sandals, carrying an umbrella, having pupils carry oil-tubes, honey, molasses and the like, and surrounded by pupils; one goes having fulfilled the duties of a traveller, carrying one's own bowl and robe, performing the duties in each monastery entered on the way, with few belongings and the utmost frugality. Before entering that monastery one has a tooth-stick made allowable on the way and takes it in; one should not first go into another cell, thinking to rest a moment, wash and anoint the feet and then go to the teacher, because monks there unfriendly to the teacher might ask the reason for coming, speak against the teacher and say "you are lost if you go to him", causing regret so that one turns back.

One should not set out with feet washed and anointed, wearing sandals, carrying an umbrella, having pupils carry oil-tubes, honey, molasses and the like, and surrounded by pupils; one goes having fulfilled the duties of a traveller, carrying one's own bowl and robe, performing the duties in each monastery entered on the way, with few belongings and the utmost frugality. Before entering that monastery one has a tooth-stick made allowable on the way and takes it in; one should not first go into another cell, thinking to rest a moment, wash and anoint the feet and then go to the teacher, because monks there unfriendly to the teacher might ask the reason for coming, speak against the teacher and say "you are lost if you go to him", causing regret so that one turns back.

paraphrase: The six temperaments are the greedy, hating, deluded, faithful, intelligent and speculative person. The commentator gives the affinity of three pairs. In the greedy person faith is strong when wholesome states occur, because faith is a near-kin quality of greed: as greed is sticky and not too rough on the unwholesome side, so is faith on the wholesome; as greed seeks sensual objects, faith seeks the virtues; as greed does not give up what harms, faith does not give up what benefits. So the faithful temperament is akin to the greedy. In the hating person understanding is strong, since it is a near-kin of hate: hate does not cling to an object, nor does understanding; hate looks for faults even where none, understanding looks for real faults; hate turns away from beings, understanding from formations. So the intelligent temperament is akin to the hating. In the deluded person, striving to arouse wholesome states, obstructing thoughts mostly arise, since thinking is close to delusion: delusion is unsettled through confusion, thinking through varied thinking; delusion wavers for lack of depth, thinking through quick imagining. So the speculative temperament is akin to the deluded.
speaker: Buddhaghosa (author of the commentary; quotations from the discourses are marked as such)

paraphrase: The commentator's verdict. Because not everyone who did much good conduct or fell from heaven is greedy, nor the others deluded, and because there is no fixed preponderance of the elements as stated, and because the humour-account names only two (greed and delusion) and contradicts itself, and because no cause is given for the faithful and so on, all this is left undecided; the reasoning of the Commentary teachers is given instead. Beings differ by preponderance (ussada) of greed, hate, delusion or of non-greed, non-hate, non-delusion, fixed by the earlier cause. When at the moment of accumulating kamma greed is strong and non-greed weak, and non-hate and non-delusion strong, hate and delusion weak, the weak non-greed cannot overcome greed but the strong ones do overcome hate and delusion; so the person is born greedy, easy-natured, not angry, and wise, with diamond-like knowledge; other combinations give other results, e.g. greedy and hating but wise like the elder Dattābhaya.

paraphrase: The scheme continues through the other combinations (for instance, one strong in non-greed, hate and delusion is free of greed and little defiled but hating and dull; one strong in all three of non-greed, non-hate and non-delusion is not greedy, not hating, and wise, like the elder Mahāsaṅgharakkhita). In this, the "greedy" is the greedy temperament; the hating and dull are the hating and deluded temperaments; the wise is the intelligent temperament; those neither greedy nor hating, of a pleasant nature, are the faithful. The one born of kamma with a following of faith is the faithful; with a following of sensual thoughts, the speculative; with a following mixed of greed and the rest, the mixed. So kamma with the retinue of one of greed and so on that gives rebirth-linking is to be understood as the cause of the temperaments.

paraphrase: How temperaments are known. A verse gives five means: from posture (iriyāpatha), from work (kicca), from eating (bhojana), from seeing (dassana) and so on, and from the arising of states (dhammappavatti). By posture: the greedy person, walking naturally, goes gracefully, puts the foot down slowly and evenly, lifts it evenly, and his footprint is "raised" (ukkuṭika). The hating person walks as if digging with the toe-tips, puts the foot down abruptly, lifts it abruptly, and his footprint is dragged along (anukaḍḍhita). The deluded person walks in a bewildered gait, puts the foot down as if startled, lifts it as if startled, and (continued on p. 105).

translation_basis: own paraphrase made directly from the Pali (IAST) text of the PTS edition; no published translation consulted

The way the Commentaries give is to be relied on: a teacher with knowledge of others' minds knows the temperament; otherwise the pupil is asked.

paraphrase: Posture (iriyāpatha) continued. The deluded person's footprint is abruptly pressed. A verse from the Māgandiya-sutta occasion says: for one with passion the footprint is "raised"; for the hating it is dragged along; for the deluded it is abruptly pressed; for one whose veil is drawn back it is such (as that of a Buddha). Even the manner of standing (māna) is pleasing and sweet-looking in the greedy, rigid in the hating, confused in the deluded; so it is in sitting. In lying down: the greedy, unhurried, lays out the bed evenly, lies down slowly with limbs gathered in a pleasing way, and when woken rises quickly and answers slowly as if in doubt. The hating, hurried, lays out the bed anyhow, throws himself down with a frown, and when woken rises quickly and answers as if angry. The deluded lays out the bed badly, sprawls, mostly face down, and when woken makes a grunt and rises sluggishly. Those of the faithful temperament and the rest, being akin to the greedy and the rest, have the same postures.

The hating person takes a hard grip on the broom, sweeps in a hurry, throwing sand up on both sides with a harsh noise, leaving it unclean and uneven. The deluded person holds the broom loosely and sweeps turning it round and stirring it up, unclean and uneven. As in sweeping, so in washing and dyeing robes and all work.

paraphrase: Eating (bhojana). The greedy person likes rich and sweet food; eating, he makes a moderate round mouthful, tastes the various flavours unhurried, and is glad if he gets something nice. The hating person likes rough and sour food; he makes a mouthful that fills the mouth, tastes nothing much, eats in a hurry, and is displeased if he gets something unpleasant. The deluded has no fixed taste; eating, he makes an untidy small mouthful, drops food in the bowl, smears his mouth, and eats with a distracted mind thinking of this and that. The faithful and the rest are to be known by following the same, being akin.

paraphrase: Seeing and so on (dassanādi). The greedy person, on seeing even a slightly pleasing sight, looks long as if amazed, clings even to a small good quality, does not take note of a real fault, and departs with reluctance and looking back. The hating person, on seeing even a slightly unpleasing sight, looks as if tired and does not look long, is offended by a small fault, does not take note of a real virtue, and departs as if wishing to be rid of it, without looking back. The deluded, on seeing whatever it is, depends on others: he blames when he hears another blame, praises when he hears praise, but himself, from ignorance, is indifferent. The same holds for hearing sounds and the rest; the faithful and the rest follow, being akin.

paraphrase: In the hating person anger, grudge, contempt, domineering, envy, avarice and the like mostly occur. In the deluded: sloth, torpor, restlessness, worry, doubt, holding tight (to views), hard to let go. In the faithful: generosity, wish to see the noble ones, wish to hear the good Dhamma, abundant gladness, uncraftiness, undeceitfulness, confidence in places that inspire it. In the intelligent: being easy to admonish, having good friends, moderation in eating, mindfulness and clear comprehension, devotion to wakefulness, a sense of urgency at what should stir it, and right striving in one so stirred. In the speculative: talkativeness, fondness for company, dislike of undertaking wholesome work, an unsettled mind, "smoking by night, blazing by day", and rushing hither and thither.

paraphrase: The commentator's own caution: this way of discerning temperament in every detail comes neither in the Pāḷi nor in the Commentary, but only according to the teachers' opinion, so it is not to be relied on as essential. Postures and so on described for the greedy can also be done by the hating and others who dwell diligently; and in a person of mixed temperament the differing marks of posture and so on do not appear together. What is stated in the Commentaries as the way to discern temperament is to be relied on: a teacher with the knowledge of others' minds will know it and give the subject, while another should ask the pupil. Hence one should know either by that knowledge or by asking the person whether he is greedy or of another temperament.

paraphrase: What suits each temperament, beginning with lodging (senāsana). For the greedy person the suitable lodging is one of these: one with an unwashed sill standing level with the ground, an unprepared rock overhang, a grass hut, a leaf hut or the like; dusty, full of bats, dilapidated, too high or too low, in bleak surroundings, threatened by dangers, unclean, with an uneven path, where even the bed and stool are full of bugs, ugly and of poor colour, so that merely looking at it brings disgust. paraphrase: What suits the greedy person, continued. Lodging where bed and stool are bug-ridden, ugly and of poor colour, so that the mere sight brings disgust. Inner and outer robes with torn edges, hanging threads, like a net-cake, rough to the touch like hemp, dirty, heavy and hard to keep. A bowl ugly in colour: a clay bowl, or an iron bowl disfigured by pins and knots, heavy, ill-shaped and repulsive like a skull. An alms-route that is disagreeable, not near a village, uneven. An alms-village where people go about as if they did not see him; where, when he leaves a house without getting alms, they say "come, venerable sir", take him into the sitting hall, give gruel and rice, and go off without looking back, as if they had put cattle into a pen. Servers who are slaves or workers, ugly, unsightly, dirty-clothed, foul-smelling, disgusting, who serve gruel and rice disrespectfully as if throwing it away. Gruel, rice and hard food that is rough and ugly: millet, kudrūsa grain, broken rice and the like, stale buttermilk, sour gruel, soup of old vegetables, anything that merely fills the belly. Posture: standing or walking. Object: any of the colour kasiṇas, blue and the rest, that is of impure colour. All this suits the greedy temperament.

paraphrase: What suits the hating person, continued. Furnishing of the lodging not too many (to limit the lodging of bugs, rats and the like): one bed and stool. His robes of the best cloths (silk, fine cotton, linen and so on), light, of one or two layers, suited to a monk, well dyed and clean in colour. His bowl well shaped like a water bubble, polished like a jewel, spotless, an iron bowl of very pure colour. The alms-route free of danger, level, pleasant, not too far and not too near a village; the alms-village where people, saying "the venerable one will come now", arrange a seat in a sprinkled and swept place, come out to meet him, take his bowl, seat him and serve him themselves with respect. His servers good-looking, pleasing, well bathed and anointed, scented with incense and flowers, in varied clean and pleasing clothes and ornaments, respectful. Food of good colour, smell and taste, nourishing, pleasing, in every way excellent, as much as needed. Posture: lying down or sitting. Object: any of the colour kasiṇas of very pure colour. This suits the hating person.

paraphrase: What suits the speculative person. A lodging that opens toward a direction where, as he sits, pleasant parks, groves and lotus ponds, a succession of villages, towns and districts, and blue-shining mountains can be seen does not suit him, because it becomes a cause of his thoughts running about. So he should live in a lodging such as a deep cave-mouth screened by forest, like the Hatthikucchi Overhang or Mahinda's Cave. A large object is not suitable, for it would be a cause of the running about of thought; a small one is suitable. The rest is as said for the greedy person.

paraphrase: This is the exposition, under "suited to one's own temperament", of the differences, causes, discernment and suitable conditions of the temperaments; but the subject suited to each is not yet shown in full, for that will become clear in the exposition of the next heading. So the forty subjects are to be decided by ten ways: by enumeration, by what brings access or absorption, by kind of jhāna, by transcending, by increase or not, by object, by plane, by taking, by condition, and by suitability to temperament. Enumeration: the forty are ten kasiṇas, ten foulnesses, ten recollections, four divine abidings, four immaterial states, one perception, one defining; and the kasiṇas begin to be listed (earth, water, fire, air, blue, yellow, red, white, light, limited space; then the ten foulnesses: bloated, livid, festering, cut up, gnawed, scattered, hacked and scattered, bleeding, worm-infested, skeleton; the recollections begin with Buddha, Dhamma, Saṅgha, virtue, generosity, deities, death, mindfulness occupied with the body, breathing, peace).

paraphrase: Which bring access only and which absorption. Ten subjects bring access only: the eight recollections other than mindfulness occupied with the body and mindfulness of breathing, the perception of repulsiveness in nutriment, and the defining of the four elements; the rest bring absorption. By kind of jhāna: the ten kasiṇas with breathing are of four jhānas (fourfold count); the ten foulnesses with the body-mindfulness are of the first jhāna; the first three divine abidings of three jhānas; the fourth divine abiding and the four immaterial states are, as this edition prints, "catukkajjhānikā". By transcending: in subjects of three or four jhānas there is transcending of factors (applied and sustained thought and so on) with the same objects; in the fourth divine abiding also (joy is left behind); in the four immaterial states there is transcending of the object.
speaker: Buddhaghosa (author of the commentary; quotations from the discourses are marked as such)
translation_basis: own paraphrase made directly from the Pali (IAST) text of the PTS edition; no published translation consulted

paraphrase: Suitability to temperament, as the text sets it out. For the greedy temperament eleven subjects suit: the ten foulnesses and mindfulness occupied with the body. For the hating temperament eight: the four divine abidings and the four colour kasiṇas. For the deluded and the speculative temperaments, one only: mindfulness of breathing. For the faithful, the first six recollections. For the intelligent, four: mindfulness of death, the recollection of peace, the defining of the four elements, and the perception of repulsiveness in nutriment. The remaining kasiṇas and the four immaterial states suit all temperaments. Among the kasiṇas any small one suits the speculative and any measureless one the deluded.

paraphrase: On the word "having taken" (gahetvā). The meditator, having approached a good friend as described, should ask for the meditation subject with a well-formed intention and resolve, first surrendering himself (attā niyyātetabbo) to the Buddha or to his teacher. To the Buddha: "Blessed One, I give up this self of mine to you." If he has not done so and lives in remote lodgings, he may be unable to stand fast when a terrifying object comes within range; he may go back to the village, mix with householders, take wrong ways of seeking, and meet misfortune. For one who has surrendered himself, fear does not arise when a terrifying object appears.

paraphrase: On the beneficial result of that surrender. When the meditator considers "I have already given this self to the Buddhas", gladness alone arises, like a man who has fine Benares cloth eaten by mice or insects and feels displeasure, but if he gives it to a monk with no robe and sees the monk cutting it up, feels only gladness. So too for the teacher: one says "Venerable sir, I give up this self to you". One who has not surrendered himself is hard to admonish, unyielding, self-willed, goes where he pleases without asking his teacher; the teacher does not help such a one with material things or Dhamma nor teach him the secret texts, and lacking both kinds of help he finds no footing in the dispensation and soon comes to bad conduct or lay life. (The passage continues on p. 116.)

paraphrase: The teacher should teach in three ways: to one who has learned the subject before, give it in one or two sittings for recitation; to one living near, teach it whenever he comes; to one who has learned and wishes to go elsewhere, teach neither too briefly nor too fully. For the earth kasiṇa, nine matters are taught: the four faults of the kasiṇa, making it, the method of developing what is made, the twofold sign, twofold concentration, sevenfold suitability and unsuitability, tenfold skill in absorption, balancing energy, and the way of absorption. For other subjects too what fits each is taught; all this will appear in the method of development for each.

paraphrase: Concluding the chapter. The meditator, while the subject is being taught, should take the sign and listen: "this is the earlier word, this the later, this is its meaning, this its intention, this its simile", binding it in each aspect; one who listens carefully in this way gets the subject well grasped, and through it attains distinction, not otherwise. paraphrase: Earth-kasiṇa: taking the learning sign. The eyes are to be opened neither too wide (the eye tires, the disk becomes too obvious and the sign does not arise) nor too little (the disk is unclear and the mind becomes sluggish, and again the sign does not arise); one opens them evenly, like one looking at the reflection of one's face in a mirror, and takes the sign. The colour is not to be reviewed nor the characteristic attended to; but without letting go of the colour, treating it as belonging to its support, one sets the mind on the concept (paññatti) as the prominent thing and attends to that. Of the names for earth (pathavī, mahī, medinī, bhūmi, vasudhā, vasundharā) one uses whichever suits one's perception, though "earth" (pathavī) is the most evident, so one develops it as "earth, earth". One adverts to it, opening the eyes at times and closing them at times, a hundred or a thousand times or more, until the learning sign (uggahanimitta) arises: it has arisen when, adverting with the eyes closed, it comes into focus just as with them open. From then on one does not sit on that spot but goes to one's own dwelling and develops it sitting there; to avoid the bother of washing the feet one should have a single-soled sandal and a staff. If the young concentration is lost through some unsuitable cause, one puts on the sandals, takes the staff, goes to the place, takes the sign, returns, sits comfortably and develops it, adverting to it again and again and striking at it with thought and applied thought. As one does so, gradually the hindrances (nīvaraṇa) are suppressed, the defilements subside, the mind is concentrated by access concentration, and the counterpart sign (paṭibhāganimitta) arises. (The text continues on p. 126 with how the two signs differ.)

paraphrase: Absorption lasts a single moment of consciousness; then comes the life-continuum (bhavanga); then, after cutting off the life-continuum, adverting for the sake of reviewing the jhāna, then the reviewing. At this point, with the formula "quite secluded from sensual desires, secluded from unwholesome states, he enters and abides in the first jhāna, with applied and sustained thought, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion", the meditator has attained the first jhāna on the earth kasiṇa, abandoning five factors, possessed of five factors, good in three ways and endowed with ten marks.

paraphrase: Commentary on "quite secluded from sensual desires" (vivicc' eva kāmehi): "having separated from sensual desires", having become without them, having withdrawn. The word "eva" is restrictive. Because it is restrictive, even though sensual desires are absent when one abides in that first jhāna, it shows that they are the opposite of the jhāna and that the jhāna is attained by giving up sensual desires alone: just as a lamp's light shows that darkness is the opposite and is present when light is absent, and reaching the far bank comes by leaving the near bank. So the "eva" makes the restriction.

paraphrase: Why "eva" is said only in the first phrase. The commentator answers that it is said there because of the escape (nissaraṇa): this jhāna is the way out of the sense sphere and the opposite of sensual lust, and so it is the very escape from sensual desires; he quotes "this is the escape from sensual desires, namely renunciation (nekkhamma)". paraphrase: The "eva" should be understood as applying also to the second phrase ("quite secluded from unwholesome states"), as in "here alone, monks, is the first ascetic, here the second". One cannot enter the jhāna without being secluded also from the other unwholesome states called the hindrances (nīvaraṇa); so both phrases have the restriction. Although the general word "secluded" covers all seclusions (by substitution of opposite, of mind, and so on), here only three are to be understood: bodily seclusion (kāyaviveka), mental seclusion (cittaviveka) and seclusion by suppression (vikkhambhanaviveka).

paraphrase: On "sensual desires" (kāmehi): the word takes in both objective sensual desires (vatthukāma: agreeable, dear sights and the rest as the Niddesa gives them) and sensual desires as defilements (kilesakāma: zeal, lust, zealous lust, intention, lust for sense objects and so on, as the Vibhaṅga gives them). So "secluded from sensual desires" is right in the sense of objective desires too, giving bodily seclusion; "secluded from unwholesome states" is right in the sense of defilement-desires or of all unwholesome states, giving mental seclusion. The first gives up the pleasure of sensuality; the second takes up the happiness of renunciation. The first also gives up the ground of defilement and the cause of fickleness and purifies the undertaking; the second gives up defilement and the cause of foolishness and nurtures the disposition. This is the method for objective sensual desires; on the side of defilement-desire, "sensual desire" (kāmacchanda) of many kinds, such as "zeal" and "lust", is meant by the single word.

paraphrase: On the "unwholesome states" that the second phrase names: sensual desire, though included among the unwholesome, is stated separately in the Vibhaṅga as opposed to the jhāna (or because it is a defilement-desire in the first phrase and an unwholesome state in the second). Of the other unwholesome states, only the hindrances (nīvaraṇa) are named, since the Vibhaṅga, in its passage on the unwholesome states ("sensual desire" and so on), shows only the hindrances, because they are the adversaries and opposites of the jhāna factors. The hindrances are opponents of the jhāna factors: they are what strike at, harm and destroy them. So it is said in the Peṭaka: concentration is the opponent of sensual desire (kāmacchanda), rapture of ill will (vyāpāda), applied thought (vitakka) of sloth and torpor (thīnamiddha), happiness (sukha) of restlessness and remorse (uddhacca-kukkucca), and sustained thought (vicāra) of doubt (vicikicchā).

paraphrase: Reading the two phrases together. "Quite secluded from sensual desires" declares the seclusion of suppression (vikkhambhana) of sensual desire (kāmacchanda); "secluded from unwholesome states" refers to all five hindrances, with the first phrase (taking what was not yet taken) covering sensual desire and the second the remaining hindrances. Likewise the first covers greed (lobha, whose object is the five cords of sensual pleasure) among the three unwholesome roots, the second hate and delusion, whose objects are the grounds of resentment and the like. Among floods, yokes, taints, clingings, bodily ties and fetters, the first covers the sensual ones (flood of sensuality, yoke of sensuality, taint of sensuality, clinging to sensuality, the bodily tie of covetousness, the fetter of sensual lust), the second the remainder; the first covers craving and what is associated with it, the second ignorance and what is associated with it; and the first the eight thought-moments associated with greed, the second the other four unwholesome kinds.

paraphrase: On "with applied thought and sustained thought" (savitakkaṃ savicāraṃ). Applied thought (vitakka) is thinking, i.e. directing (ūhana). Its mark is the directing of consciousness onto an object; its function is striking and threshing (the meditator makes the object struck and threshed by applied thought); its manifestation is leading consciousness onto the object. Sustained thought (vicāra) is roving, i.e. continued moving about. Its mark is continued pondering (anumajjana) of the object; its function is to keep the conascent states on it; its manifestation is consciousness's continued binding to it. Though the two are not always separate, applied thought is coarser and comes first, like the striking of a bell; sustained thought is subtler, like the ringing that follows. Applied thought is a stirring of consciousness at first arising, like a bird about to fly spreading its wings, or a bee heading for a lotus; sustained thought is the calm, unagitated occurring, like the bird gliding on outspread wings or the bee hovering above the lotus.

paraphrase: "Rapture and happiness" (pītisukha). Rapture (pīti) is so called because it refreshes. Its mark is being endeared (sampiyāyana); its function is to refresh body and mind, or to pervade; its manifestation is elation. It is fivefold: minor rapture (khuddikā), momentary (khaṇikā), showering (okkantikā), uplifting (ubbegā) and pervading (pharaṇā).

paraphrase: The five kinds described. Minor rapture can raise the hairs on the body only. Momentary rapture comes at moments like flashes of lightning. Showering rapture breaks over the body again and again like waves on a seashore. Uplifting rapture is strong, lifting the body up until it leaps into the air; the elder Mahā-Tissa of Puṇṇavallika, on a full-moon evening, seeing the moonlight and turning toward the Great Shrine, thought of the four assemblies paying homage there, produced uplifting rapture with the Buddha as object, and leapt like a ball into the air and landed in the shrine courtyard.

paraphrase: The girl of Vattakālaka village at Girikaṇḍaka (continued from p. 143): her parents, going to hear the Dhamma, told her, being "heavy-burdened" (garubhārā), that she could not go about at the wrong time; from the house terrace she saw the shrine courtyard by moonlight, the lamp-offering and the four assemblies with the monks reciting, and thought them fortunate; uplifting rapture arose in her, she leapt through the air, and arrived at the shrine before her parents. This fivefold rapture, as it grows and matures, fulfils twofold tranquillity (passaddhi), of body and of consciousness; tranquillity, growing and maturing, fulfils twofold happiness, bodily and mental; happiness, growing and maturing, fulfils threefold concentration: momentary, access and absorption. Of these, the pervading rapture that grows and becomes the root of absorption concentration and joins with concentration is the rapture meant in this sense.

paraphrase: Happiness (sukha) is so called because it makes easy and gulps down (khādati) or digs out (khaṇati) bodily and mental affliction. Its mark is gratification (sāta); its function is to enhance the associated states; its manifestation is aiding. Though rapture and happiness are not always separate, rapture is the gladness at getting a desirable object, happiness the experiencing of what is got. Where there is rapture there is happiness; where there is happiness there is not necessarily rapture. Rapture belongs to the formations aggregate, happiness to the feeling aggregate. Rapture is like a traveller weary in the desert who hears or sees water in the woods; happiness is like his entering the shade and using the water. They are shown in different moments where each is prominent. So this jhāna is "with rapture and happiness" in that both belong to it, or is "rapture-and-happiness born of seclusion" as one compound, both born of seclusion.

paraphrase: On "with five factors abandoned": the abandoned factors are the five hindrances (nīvaraṇa): sensual desire (kāmacchanda), ill will (vyāpāda), sloth and torpor (thīnamiddha), restlessness and remorse (uddhacca-kukkucca) and doubt (vicikicchā). The jhāna does not arise while these are unabandoned, so they are called the factors of abandoning. Though other unwholesome states are also abandoned at the moment of jhāna, these five in particular are the obstructions to jhāna. Consciousness enticed by objects of many kinds is not concentrated on a unified object; overcome by sensual desire it does not follow the way to abandon the sense sphere. Struck by ill will at the object it does not continue without a break. Overcome by sloth and torpor it becomes unwieldy. Overtaken by restlessness and remorse it is unquiet and wanders about. Harmed by doubt it does not climb the way that leads to attaining the jhāna.

paraphrase: On "possessed of five factors": since applied thought directs consciousness onto the object, sustained thought binds it on, and for consciousness thus prepared to be undistracted, rapture (from success of the endeavour) refreshes and happiness enhances, then one-pointedness, aided by these, steadies the mind with its associated states evenly and rightly on a single object. So the five factors are applied thought (vitakka), sustained thought (vicāra), rapture (pīti), happiness (sukha) and one-pointedness of mind (cittekaggatā); when these five have arisen the jhāna has arisen. It is not that some other jhāna has these five: as a four-limbed army, a five-piece band and the eightfold path are named by their limbs only, so the jhāna is called "five-limbed" by the mere factors. (Continues on p. 147.)

paraphrase: The five factors are present in access too, but there they are stronger than ordinary consciousness; here (in the first jhāna) they are stronger even than in access and reach the character of the fine-material sphere. Applied thought arises directing consciousness on the object in a very purified way; sustained thought pondering the object exceedingly; rapture and happiness pervading the whole body; as the discourse says, "there is nothing in his whole body that is not pervaded by the rapture and happiness born of seclusion." One-pointedness, though not named in the wording "with applied and sustained thought", is a factor, since the Vibhaṅga says "jhāna is applied thought, sustained thought, rapture, happiness, one-pointedness of mind": the intention of the Blessed One's summary is shown by his own analysis.

paraphrase: On "good in three ways, endowed with ten marks": the jhāna is good in beginning, middle and end, and the ten marks are the marks of those three. The Pāḷi says: the purification of the way (paṭipadā-visuddhi) is the beginning of the first jhāna; the strengthening by onlooking equanimity (upekkhānubrūhaṇā) is the middle; gladdening (sampahaṃsanā) is the end. The beginning has three marks: the consciousness is purified of the obstruction to it; being purified, it enters on the middle sign of calm; having entered, it leaps forward there. So the first jhāna is good in the beginning and possessed of these three marks. (The middle and end are given on p. 148.)

Mindful he breathes in, mindful he breathes out; breathing in long he knows "I breathe in long", breathing out long he knows "I breathe out long"; likewise short; he trains "I shall breathe in, breathe out, experiencing the whole body" and "calming the bodily formation"; and so on through rapture (pīti), happiness (sukha), the mental formation (cittasankhāra), calming the mental formation, experiencing the mind, gladdening the mind, concentrating the mind, liberating the mind, contemplating impermanence, dispassion, cessation and relinquishment; the text gives these as the sixteen-based subject of mindfulness of breathing.

paraphrase: "Peaceful and sublime": this concentration is peaceful (santo) and sublime (paṇīto) both by object and by factor, unlike the foulness subject which is peaceful and sublime only by penetration but is neither by object, since its object is gross and repulsive; it is never in any way unpeaceful or unsublime and gives no satiety. "Unadulterated and a pleasant abiding": it is unmixed, needing neither preparatory work nor access for its peacefulness, being peaceful and sublime by its own nature from the first attention; some say "unadulterated" is "not sprinkled, sweet by itself". It brings bodily and mental pleasure at each moment of attainment. "Arisen, arisen": those not yet suppressed. "Evil": inferior. "Unwholesome states": those born of unskilfulness. "At once": in a moment, it suppresses them; "subsides": calms them well, or, being of the penetrating sort, it in due course cuts them off with the growth of the noble path. The commentator gives the brief sense: by what means and in what manner, by what method is the concentration of mindfulness of breathing developed and made much of so that it is peaceful and sublime?

paraphrase: On "here, monks, a monk": "here" points to the dispensation in which the person who can bring about the concentration of mindfulness of breathing in all its ways relies, and excludes other dispensations, as in the saying "only here, monks, is the ascetic; others are empty of ascetics". "Gone to the forest ... or to an empty place": this shows the choice of a dwelling fit for developing this concentration. The mind of such a monk has long wandered among objects such as forms and does not wish to climb onto the object of mindfulness of breathing; like a cart yoked to a vicious ox it runs off the road.

paraphrase: The simile continued: as a cowherd wishing to tame a calf reared on the milk of a vicious cow takes it from the cow, plants a big post at one side and ties it to it, so that after struggling this way and that it cannot flee and settles down or lies down by the post, the monk wishing to tame his wrongly-disposed mind, long nourished on the taste of forms and other objects, takes it away from those objects and brings it into a forest, to a tree root or an empty place, and ties it with the rope of mindfulness to the post of the in- and out-breath. Then, unable to get its former objects and unable to cut the rope of mindfulness and flee, it settles down and lies down by that very object by way of access and absorption. The ancients said: as one ties the calf to the post to tame it, so should one tie one's own mind firmly to the object with mindfulness. In this way the dwelling is fit for development.

translation_basis: own paraphrase made directly from the Pali (IAST) text of the PTS edition; no published translation consulted

paraphrase: A second reason for the forest: this subject of mindfulness of breathing, which stands at the head of the subjects, is the base for the distinctions attained by the fully awakened Buddhas, the paccekabuddhas and the Buddha's disciples and for their pleasant abiding here and now; it is not easy to develop without leaving the village's edge, which is crowded with the sounds of women, men, elephants, horses and the like, sound being a thorn to jhāna; in a forest with no village, it is easy for the meditator to take the subject, produce the four jhānas of breathing, make that the base, comprehend the formations and reach the highest fruit, arahatship. So, showing a dwelling fit for it, the Blessed One said "gone to the forest" and so on. The Blessed One is like an expert in sites (continued on p. 270).
speaker: Buddhaghosa (author of the commentary; quotations from the discourses are marked as such)

notes: The fourfold jhāna of breathing is the fourfold reckoning given in the text; "comprehend the formations" refers to insight founded on the jhāna.

paraphrase: The simile continued: as a site-expert examines the ground for a city and says "build the city here", and, when the city is safely finished, is honoured by the royal house, so the Buddha examines a fit dwelling for the meditator and says "practise the subject here"; when the meditator, practising, reaches arahatship, people honour the Buddha: "he is truly the Fully Awakened, the Blessed One". Also this monk is compared to a leopard: as a great leopard hides in thickets, woods or mountain thickets and seizes forest buffaloes, deer and pigs, so the monk who practises in the forest and elsewhere gradually seizes the paths of stream-entry, once-return, non-return and arahatship and the noble fruits. The ancients said: the leopard hides and seizes deer; so the Buddha's son, devoted, an insight-meditator, enters the forest and seizes the supreme fruit.

paraphrase: Showing the forest lodging as a ground fit for the speed of his exertion, the Blessed One said "gone to the forest". "Forest" is defined: outside the boundary stone, all this is forest; a forest lodging is one at least five hundred bow-lengths (from the village); so "gone to the forest" means gone to any forest of these stated marks where the happiness of seclusion is found. "Gone to the root of a tree" means gone near a tree. "Gone to an empty place" means gone to an empty, secluded spot; apart from forest and tree-root, one who has gone to any of the remaining seven kinds of lodging may be said to have "gone to an empty place".

paraphrase: Having pointed to a lodging that suits the three seasons and the temperament of the (bodily) elements, the Blessed One then said "sits down", indicating a posture that is peaceful and inclined neither to sluggishness nor to restlessness. To show that the sitting is firm, that the breathing goes easily, and how to fix the object, he said "folding his legs crosswise". "Cross-legged" (pallanka) is sitting with the thighs locked all round; "folding" is binding. "Having set the body erect" is holding the upper body straight, the eighteen vertebrae end to end; for one who sits so, skin, flesh and sinews do not bend, and so the feelings that would arise at each moment from their bending do not arise; the mind is well concentrated, the subject does not fall away and it grows and flourishes.
speaker: Buddhaghosa (author of the commentary; quotations from the discourses are marked as such)
translation_basis: own paraphrase made directly from the Pali (IAST) text of the PTS edition; no published translation consulted

paraphrase: "Establishing mindfulness in front": setting mindfulness toward the meditation subject; or, as the Paṭisambhidā has it, pari = embracing, mukha = outlet, sati = establishing, so mindfulness made to embrace and lead out. "He breathes in mindful, breathes out mindful": the monk, seated so and having established mindfulness, not letting go of it, breathes in and out with mindfulness alone, acting mindfully. The text cites the Paṭisambhidā's analysis of this: he is "one who acts mindfully" in thirty-two ways, since by way of the long in-breath, the long out-breath and so on through the sixteen steps, in-breath and out-breath, mindfulness is established in one who knows the concentrated, undistracted state of mind.

paraphrase: "Long" and "short". The Vinaya commentary says assāsa is the wind going out and passāsa the wind coming in, while the discourse commentaries give the reverse order. For all beings born from the womb, when leaving the mother's womb, the inner wind first goes out and then the outer wind, carrying fine dust, goes in and, striking the palate, ceases. The long and short are known by duration (addhāna): as water or sand spread over a space is called long water or long sand, or short, so breaths in an elephant's or a snake's body fill the long extent of that body slowly and go out slowly and are called long; in a dog or hare they fill the short extent quickly and go out quickly and are called short. Among humans some breathe in and out long by time like elephants and snakes, some short like dogs and hares; the breaths that take a long time are long, those that take a little are short.

paraphrase: The other monk finds all of it clear and can grasp all, and is troubled nowhere; the Blessed One, showing that the meditator should be such, says "experiencing the whole body". "He trains" means he strives so: the restraint in one who is so is the training in higher virtue, the concentration is the training in higher mind, the understanding the training in higher understanding; in that object, with that mindfulness, with that attention he trains, practises, develops and makes much of these three. In the earlier steps he only has to breathe in and out and nothing else to do, so the text is put in the present ("he knows 'I breathe in'"); from here on effort is needed in producing knowledge and the rest, so the text is put in the future ("I shall breathe in, experiencing the whole body").

paraphrase: "Calming the bodily formation": he trains breathing in and out while calming, stilling, stopping and appeasing the gross bodily formation (the in- and out-breath). Gross and subtle, and calming: before the meditator has grasped the object, body and mind are disturbed and gross; when body and mind are gross and unappeased the breaths are gross, grow stronger and the nose is not enough, so he stands breathing in and out through the mouth. When body and mind are grasped they become calm and stilled and the breaths become subtle, so that it becomes a matter of checking "are they there or not?", like the breaths of a man who has run or come down a mountain or set down a heavy load from his head.

paraphrase: The simile continued: when he has rested, bathed, drunk and lies in cool shade with a wet cloth on his chest, the breaths become subtle and doubtful whether they exist. So too for the meditator: before grasping, there is no attending, adverting or reviewing "I calm the coarser and coarser bodily formation"; after grasping there is, so the formation becomes subtler. The ancients said: when body and mind are disturbed it goes on excessively; when the body is undisturbed it goes on subtly. The reciters differ on how the formation becomes subtle through the stages of jhāna: the Dīgha and Saṃyutta reciters say it is gross in grasping, subtle in the access of the first jhāna, gross there, subtle in the first jhāna, and so on up to the fourth jhāna, in which it is very subtle and reaches non-occurrence; the Majjhima reciters say gross in the first jhāna and subtle in the access of the second, and so on, each higher access subtler. By all agreement the formation occurring before grasping is calmed on grasping, that in each access calmed in the jhāna next above. In insight the formation is gross when unlimited by grasping, subtle when it grasps the great elements, and so on through form, mind, conditions, and the seeing of mind-and-matter with its conditions, to insight with characteristics as object, gross in weak insight and subtle in strong.

paraphrase: The Paṭisambhidā's explanation with objection and answer: the bodily formations are the in- and out-breaths, states of the body bound up with the body; calming, stopping and stilling them, he trains. Objection: if he trains in stilling all bodily movement (bending, swaying, trembling and so on), then there would be no apprehension of the wind, no knowing of the in- and out-breaths, no mindfulness of breathing and no concentration of mindfulness of breathing, and the wise would not enter or emerge from this attainment; the answer: on the contrary, in the calming the wind is known and the wise do enter and emerge. The comparison follows: when a bell is struck, first gross sounds are heard, and because the sign of the gross sounds was well grasped, well attended and well noted, after the gross sound has ceased subtle sounds arise with the sign well grasped (continued on p. 277).

paraphrase: Bell simile concluded: as gross sounds are followed by subtle sounds and then by the sign of subtle sound as object, so first gross breaths occur, then, the sign of the gross breaths being well grasped, subtle ones, and after the subtle breaths cease, the mind, having the sign of the subtle breath as object, does not go astray. Thus the breaths are the body as ground, mindfulness and knowledge contemplating, and it is called developing the establishment of mindfulness by contemplating the body in the body. This is the word-by-word commentary on the first tetrad, spoken by way of contemplating the body.

paraphrase: Since in this text the first tetrad is given as the subject for a beginner (ādikammika), while the other three tetrads are given for one who has already attained jhāna, by way of contemplating feelings, mind and mental objects, the clansman who wishes, having developed this subject, to reach arahatship together with the analytical knowledges through insight founded on the fourfold jhāna of breathing, should, having done the preliminary tasks such as purifying virtue, learn the five-link subject (pañcasandhika) from a teacher of the sort described. paraphrase: The five links explained: the characteristic is the discerning of the subject's own nature ("this subject has this characteristic"). One who learns the five-link subject neither wearies himself nor troubles his teacher; so, having had a little taught and recited it for a long time, having learned the subject in five links, he lives, whether near the teacher or elsewhere, in a fit lodging as described, having cut the minor impediments, done the meal, dispelled the drowsiness of food, sat comfortably, and gladdened his mind by recollecting the virtues of the Triple Gem; not forgetting a single word of the teacher's teaching, he attends to this subject of mindfulness of breathing.

paraphrase: The method of attention (manasikāra) has eight terms: counting (gaṇanā), connecting (anubandhanā), touching (phusanā), fixing (ṭhapanā), noting (sallakkhaṇā), turning away (vivaṭṭanā), purification (pārisuddhi), and looking back on these (paṭipassanā). Counting is counting itself; connecting is following; touching is the place touched; fixing is absorption; noting is insight; turning away is the path; purification is the fruit; looking back is reviewing. Of these, the beginner first attends by counting: he must not count fewer than five nor more than ten, and must not make a gap in between. If he stops below five, consciousness struggles in a confined space, like a herd of cattle shut in a cramped pen; if he goes above ten, consciousness comes to depend on the counting; if he breaks the count, the mind wavers ("has my subject reached its peak or not?"). So he avoids these faults. He first counts slowly, like a measurer of grain, who fills the measure, says "one", and pours it out, and when he sees some rubbish while filling again says "one, one" as he throws it away; and so for two, two and the rest; so the meditator takes whatever breath is evident and says "one, one" (continued on p. 279).

paraphrase: Counting continued. Up to "ten, ten" he counts, having noted the breath as each occurs. When the going out and coming in breaths become evident to him as he counts so, he should give up the slow counting like the grain-measurer and count quickly, in the herdsman's way: a skilful herdsman, with pebbles in the fold of his cloth and a stick in hand, goes to the pen at dawn, strikes the backs of the cattle, sits on the gate-post and counts each animal as it reaches the gate ("one, two") throwing a pebble each time; the cattle, distressed through the night in the cramped space, come out in bunches and he counts "three, four, five, ten" without stopping. So the meditator, when the breaths become evident and keep passing quickly, counts them in the herdsman's way, taking only those that reach the gate (the place touched), "one, two, three, four, five; one ... six, ... ten", quickly. For a subject bound by counting, consciousness becomes one-pointed by the power of counting, as a boat in a strong current is held by a rudder. When the subject seems to go on without break, then, not seizing the wind inside or outside, he counts as before with speed. If consciousness goes in with the inner wind, the inside seems full of wind, as if filled with fat; if it goes out with the outer wind, consciousness is scattered among many external objects; development succeeds for one who develops by setting mindfulness at the place touched.

paraphrase: The purpose of counting is only to establish mindfulness on the object of in- and out-breath by cutting off thoughts scattered outside. Having attended by counting, he attends by connecting (anubandhanā): withdrawing the counting, he follows the in- and out-breaths continuously with mindfulness, but not by following their beginning, middle and end. For the outgoing wind the navel is the beginning, the heart the middle, the nose-tip the end; for the incoming wind the nose-tip is the beginning, the heart the middle, the navel the end; and when he follows it so, his consciousness, scattered, becomes agitated and unsteady, as the text says: when he follows the beginning, middle and end of the in-breath with mindfulness, body and mind become agitated, unsteady and shaky through consciousness scattered inwardly; and likewise for the out-breath through consciousness scattered outwardly. So one who attends by connecting should not attend by beginning, middle and end, but by touching (phusanā) and fixing (ṭhapanā). There is no attention by touching and fixing separate from counting and connecting as there is between those two; counting just at the place touched, he attends by counting and touching.
speaker: Buddhaghosa (author of the commentary; quotations from the discourses are marked as such)

paraphrase: The lame man's simile concluded: he sees both ends and the middle of the swing-plank without exerting himself to see them; so the monk, seated at the post of mindfulness, pushes the swing of the in- and out-breath and, sitting there at the sign with mindfulness, follows the beginning, middle and end of the breaths at the place they touch as they come and go, fixing the mind there, and sees without exerting himself to see them. The doorkeeper simile: a doorkeeper at a city gate does not examine the people inside and outside ("who are you? where from? where going? what in your hand?") for they are not his burden, but examines only those who reach the gate; so for the monk the wind that has gone in and gone out is not the burden, only that which has reached the gate is.

paraphrase: The saw simile is to be understood from the beginning. The text quotes: "The sign, the in-breath and the out-breath are not the object of a single consciousness; for one who does not know these three things development is not obtained. The sign, the in-breath and the out-breath are not the object of a single consciousness; for one who knows these three things development is obtained." How can these three not be the object of a single consciousness, yet not be unknown, the mind not become distracted, the effort be evident, the work be done and distinction be reached? As when a log is placed on level ground and a man saws it: his mindfulness is established by the saw-teeth where they touch the log, without his attending to the teeth as they come and go, yet they are not unknown to him as they come and go; the effort is evident, the work is done and distinction is reached. As the log is, so is the sign that serves as the anchor (of mindfulness); as the saw-teeth are, so are the in- and out-breaths (the passage continues on p. 282).

As when a log is placed on level ground and a man saws it: his mindfulness is established by the saw-teeth where they touch the log, without his attending to the teeth as they come and go, yet they are not unknown to him as they come and go; the effort is evident, the work is done and distinction is reached. As the log is, so is the sign that serves as the anchor (of mindfulness); as the saw-teeth are, so are the in- and out-breaths (the passage continues on p. 282).

Both lines say the sign and the breaths are NOT the object of a single consciousness; the paraphrase makes the second line say they "are the object of one consciousness", inverting it. It also renders "upanibandhananimittaṃ" (the sign as the anchor) as "the sign of connecting".

paraphrase: Whom not to begin with. This loving-kindness is not to be developed first toward a disliked person, a very dear friend, a neutral person or an enemy; not specifically (odhiso) toward one of the opposite sex; and not at all toward one who is dead. Reasons: setting a disliked person in the place of a dear one is tiring; setting a very dear friend in the place of a neutral one is tiring, and when even a small pain comes to him one is as if weeping; a neutral person put in the place of a respected or dear one is tiring; recalling an enemy brings anger. Toward the opposite sex, desire (rāga) arises: a minister's son asked an elder toward whom to develop loving-kindness, was told "a dear person", took his own wife, and fought a wall-battle all night. Toward the dead one reaches neither absorption nor access: a young monk who developed it toward his teacher could not enter absorption until he found the "sign", learned that his teacher was dead, and took another person as object.

paraphrase: The order. So, for the sake of the witness-state, one first pervades oneself with loving-kindness, then, for the occurring of happiness, one develops it toward a person who is dear and agreeable, a teacher or one like a teacher, a preceptor or one like a preceptor, recalling his endearing words and the virtue and learning that make him dear and respected: "may this good man be happy and free from suffering". Absorption comes about easily in such a person. But the bhikkhu who wishes to break down the barriers (sīmasambheda) must not be content with that; next he develops it toward a very dear friend, from him toward a neutral person, and from the neutral toward an enemy. At each step he should make the mind soft and workable in one part before extending to the next. One who has no enemy, or who, being of great nature, has no perception of an enemy even when wronged, need not strive to produce one.

paraphrase: The seventh thing: the enemy wishes "may he, at the breaking up of the body after death, not go to a good destination, heaven"; but an angry man does bad deeds in body, speech and mind and, after death, is reborn in a bad destination, hell. The angry man is like a torch burnt at both ends and smeared with dung in the middle, useless as timber either in village or forest. The meditator tells himself that, being angry, he is not doing the Blessed One's teaching, is worse than the one who returns anger and will not win the hard battle, and will himself do what pleases his enemies; he will be like the burnt torch. If the resentment subsides, well; if not, he should recall whatever quality in that person is calm and pure, which brings confidence when recalled, and by it dispel the anger.

paraphrase: Mental conduct as the calm quality: in one person only the mental conduct is calm, and this shows in all when he pays homage at a shrine and so on. One whose mind is not calm pays homage to the shrine, the Bodhi tree or the elders carelessly, and sits in the Dhamma hall distracted or nodding; the calm-minded pays homage attentively and listens to the Dhamma with a purposeful mind, showing confidence by body or speech. If in a person none of the three is calm, compassion (kāruñña) should be set up toward him: "though he now walks the world of men, in a few days he will be filling the eight great hells and the sixteen extra hells"; for compassion too dispels resentment. If all three are calm, he may recall any of them, since loving-kindness toward such a person is not difficult. For the fuller meaning the Āghātapaṭivinaya-sutta in the Book of Fives is to be expanded, which gives five ways by which a resentment that has arisen in a bhikkhu is to be entirely removed.

paraphrase: If resentment still arises, the meditator should admonish himself with verses. In sum: if an enemy has done you harm in his own domain, why do you want to do harm in your own mind's domain? Having left your kin who helped you much, with a weeping face, why do you not give up anger, the great cause of harm, your enemy? Anger cuts the root of the virtues you guard; who is as foolish as you to pet it? If another has done a wrong deed and you are angry at that, do you yourself want to do the same? If another has done what is disagreeable to you wishing to hurt you, why fulfil his wish by making hate arise in yourself? Whether or not you will make him suffer by your anger, you afflict yourself now with the pain of anger. If enemies have taken the harmful road of anger, why are you following them in anger? Cut the very fault in you because of which your enemy did what displeases you: why torment yourself for no reason?

paraphrase: If resentment does not subside even so, the meditator should reflect on the ownership of kamma, his own and the other's. His own: "What will you achieve by being angry with him? Does not this kamma, rooted in hate, lead to your own harm? You are the owner of your kamma, heir to your kamma, born of kamma, kin to kamma, with kamma as refuge; whatever kamma you do you will inherit. This kamma of yours is not able to bring about awakening, private awakening, the disciple's stage, Brahmā-hood, Sakka-hood, universal kingship, or any such attainment; it leads to losing the dispensation and to being a scrap-eater and to various sufferings of hell and the like; in doing it you are like a man who seizes glowing coals or dung with both hands to strike another, burning and befouling yourself first." The other's kamma is to be reflected on the same way: he too is owner of his kamma; what he does will bring harm to himself, like a man throwing dust against the wind.

paraphrase: The Buddha's verse: who offends an innocent, pure, blameless man, that evil comes back on that very fool like fine dust thrown against the wind. If even so the resentment does not subside, the meditator should recall the Teacher's earlier practice of virtue: "Monk, before his awakening, as a bodhisatta fulfilling the perfections for four incalculables and a hundred thousand eons, your Teacher did not allow his mind to hate even his murderers and enemies." In the Sīlava-jātaka, when a wicked minister who had committed an offence concerning his queen (attano deviyā paduṭṭhena) brought a rival king to take his kingdom of three hundred yojanas, he did not allow the ministers who rose up to defend him even to touch a weapon; and when he was buried with a thousand ministers up to the neck in a charnel ground he made no hatred; after being saved through the digging of jackals and, by a spirit's power, seeing his enemy asleep in the royal bedchamber, he felt no anger, exchanged oaths and made him a friend, saying: "a man should hope, the wise do not despair; I see myself as I wished."

As a great monkey rescued from a mountain pit by a man who then thought to kill and eat him, he did not hate the man, and, though his head was split by a thrown stone, looked at him with tears and said "do not do such a thing; you are one of long life and ought to restrain others", felt no hate, and led him to safety. The story of the serpent king Bhūridatta, who had undertaken the uposatha factors, begins at the foot of the page.

paraphrase: Bhūridatta, lying on an anthill observing the uposatha, was smeared over his whole body with a drug like the fire at the world's end and carried in a basket around the whole of Jambudīpa as a plaything, yet showed no ill will toward the brahmin; the text quotes his verse that, though thrown in the basket and crushed, he did not get angry from fear of breaking his virtue. Campeyya the serpent king, tormented by a snake-charmer, produced no ill will; and Saṅkhapāla the serpent king, pierced by sharp spears, dragged with a rope through his nose by sixteen hunters' sons, able to reduce them to ashes by a look, did not even open his eye in anger. Each is said to have quoted his own verse of patience as observance of virtue.

paraphrase: If the resentment still does not subside for one long enslaved by defilements, the meditator should reflect on the beginningless round: "it is not easy to find a being who has not been mother, father, brother, sister, son or daughter" (SN 15). paraphrase: If even so the mind cannot be calmed, the meditator should reflect on the benefits of loving-kindness (mettānisaṃsa): "Monk, has the Blessed One not said that eleven benefits are to be expected when the liberation of mind by loving-kindness is practised, developed, made much of, made a vehicle and a basis, established, consolidated and well undertaken? One sleeps happily; wakes happily; sees no bad dream; is dear to human beings; is dear to non-human beings; devas guard him; fire, poison and weapons do not affect him; the mind is quickly concentrated; the complexion is serene; he dies unconfused; and, if he penetrates no higher, he goes to the Brahmā world." (The list ends at the head of p. 306.)

paraphrase: With the eleventh benefit ended, the text closes the reflection: "if you do not calm this mind you will be outside these benefits." If even so the mind cannot be calmed, the meditator should analyse into the elements (dhātuvinibbhoga): "with whom are you angry, in being angry with this person? With his head hair, body hair, nails... urine? Or with the earth element in the hair and the rest, or the water, fire or air element? Or of the five aggregates, twelve sense bases and eighteen elements by which he is called 'this venerable so-and-so', are you angry with the form aggregate, or feeling, perception, formations or consciousness? With the eye base, the form base ... the mind base, the mental-object base? With the eye element ... the mind-consciousness element?" For one who does this analysis, anger has no place to stand, like a mustard seed on the tip of an awl or a picture in the air.

paraphrase: If the meditator cannot do the analysis into elements, he should practise sharing gifts (dānasaṃvibhāga): give what is his own to the other and accept what is the other's; if the other has a broken livelihood and requisites unfit for use, only his own is to be given. By doing this his resentment toward that person is surely calmed; and the other person's anger too, even if it has followed him from a past birth, subsides at that very moment, as did that of the great elder at Cittalapabbata monastery who received the bowl given by the alms-food elder whose lodging had three times been taken from him, with the words "venerable sir, this bowl worth eight kahāpaṇas was given me by my mother, the lay-woman, as a lawful gain: let the great lay-woman gain merit." The text says such is the power of giving, and quotes a verse: giving tames the untamed, giving accomplishes everything; by giving and kind speech people rise up and bow.

paraphrase: When resentment toward the enemy has subsided, the mind occurs with loving-kindness toward him as toward the dear, the very dear friend and the neutral. Then, by developing loving-kindness again and again toward himself, the dear person, the neutral person and the enemy, and making the mind equal toward these four, he should break down the barriers (sīmasambheda). The mark: suppose he sits in one place with these three (dear, neutral, enemy) and himself as the fourth, and bandits come and say "give us one bhikkhu" for a blood-offering; if he thinks "let them take so-and-so", the barrier is not broken; even if he thinks "take me, not these three", it is not broken, because he wishes the good of one and not of the others. When among the four he sees no one to give the bandits and his mind is equal toward himself and the three, the barrier is broken. The ancients' verse: so long as he sees a difference among himself, the dear, the neutral and the hostile, though his mind is of good will toward beings, he is not called skilled in loving-kindness, one who gains it at will (nikāmalābhī); when the four barriers are broken down for the bhikkhu, he pervades the whole world with its gods with loving-kindness equally, and he whose barrier is no longer known is greatly better than the former. At the moment the barrier is broken the meditator gains the sign and access; then, developing that sign, he reaches absorption with little trouble in the way said for the earth kasiṇa: the first jhāna accompanied by loving-kindness (with five factors abandoned, five possessed, good in three ways, ten marks) and, continuing, the second and third in the fourfold count (the second, third and fourth in the fivefold) (continued on p. 308).
