paraphrase: Glosses on the formula. "Accompanied by loving-kindness" means endowed with loving-kindness; "with the mind" is consciousness; "one direction" is said by way of pervading the beings included in one direction, taking first the beings delimited (in that direction); "having pervaded" is having touched (with it) and made it the object; "abides" is to keep going a posture of abiding sustained by the divine abiding. "Likewise the second" means after pervading any one direction, in the same way the second, third and fourth. "Above" is in the same way as "the earlier direction"; "below" and "across" are downward and the intermediate directions; so the mind accompanied by loving-kindness, like a horse in a horse-ring, goes and returns in all directions. This much shows the pervading of each direction, delimited (odhiso). "Everywhere" and the rest show the undelimited (anodhiso): "everywhere" is everywhere; "to all as to himself" is with the state of oneself in all the classes (the low, middling, high, friend, enemy, neutral) not making the distinction "this is another being"; or, "with the whole part of the mind", not distracted outward in the least.

paraphrase: Word-explanations and the marks of the four divine abidings. Loving-kindness (mettā) is friendliness; compassion (karuṇā) is what makes the hearts of the good tremble when others suffer, or destroys others' suffering, or is extended over the suffering; gladness (muditā) is gladness in others' good or the mere being glad; equanimity (upekkhā) is looking on with the giving up of the effort of "may they be free from hate" and coming to neutrality. By mark, function, manifestation and proximate cause: loving-kindness has as mark the occurring in the aspect of welfare; as function, bringing welfare; as manifestation, removing resentment (āghāta); as proximate cause, seeing the agreeable side of beings. Its success is the stilling of ill will; its failure is the arising of affection (sineha).

paraphrase: Compassion has as mark the occurring in the aspect of removing suffering; as function, not bearing others' suffering; as manifestation, non-cruelty; as proximate cause, seeing the helplessness of those overcome by suffering; its success is the stilling of cruelty, its failure the arising of sorrow. Gladness has as mark rejoicing; as function, non-envy; as manifestation, the removal of discontent; as proximate cause, seeing beings' success; success is the stilling of discontent, failure the arising of exhilaration (pahāsa). Equanimity has as mark the occurring in the aspect of neutrality toward beings; as function, seeing equality among beings; as manifestation, the stilling of resentment and favour; as proximate cause, seeing beings as owners of their kamma ("by whose wish will they be happy, or be freed from suffering, or not fall from the prosperity they have reached?"); success is the stilling of resentment and favour, failure the arising of the ignorant indifference of the household life. The common purpose of all four is pleasant abiding in insight and success in existence; the special purpose is the destruction of ill will and so on: loving-kindness for ill will, the others for cruelty, discontent and lust. The text quotes: "this is the escape from ill will, namely the liberation of mind by loving-kindness" and so for compassion (cruelty), gladness (discontent) and equanimity (lust). Each of the four has two enemies, near and far (continued on p. 319).

paraphrase: The near and far enemies (paccatthika). Lust (rāga) is the near enemy of loving-kindness, being like it in seeing virtues; it finds an opening quickly, so loving-kindness must be well guarded from it; ill will (vyāpāda) is the far enemy, like a man's enemy who lives hidden in mountain thickets, alike by being unlike, so one develops loving-kindness fearlessly from it; it is impossible for one who has loving-kindness to be angry. For compassion, the household-based (gehasita) displeasure that arises in one who regards non-attainment of desirable forms as non-attainment, or recalls past attainment lost and changed, is the near enemy, being like it in seeing what has gone wrong; cruelty is the far enemy. For gladness, household-based gladness at attainment is the near enemy; discontent (arati) is the far enemy. For equanimity, the household-based equanimity of the ignorant fool, who on seeing a form has an indifference that does not go beyond the form, is the near enemy, since it is like it in not considering fault and merit; lust and resentment are the far enemies.

paraphrase: Chapter XIV, on the aggregate of formations, continues with the unwholesome. In the first unwholesome consciousness rooted in greed there are seventeen: thirteen given in their own form (contact, volition, applied thought, sustained thought, rapture, energy, life faculty, concentration, shamelessness, fearlessness of wrongdoing, greed, delusion, wrong view) and four "whatever" factors (zeal, resolve, restlessness, attention). Shamelessness (ahirika) has as its mark absence of disgust at bodily misconduct and the like, or lack of conscience; fearlessness of wrongdoing (anottappa) has as its mark absence of dread of the same, or lack of fear. Greed (lobha) is that by which one is greedy, or which is greedy, or mere greed: its mark is grasping an object, like a monkey-lime; its function is sticking, like a piece of meat thrown into a hot pan; its manifestation is non-relinquishing, like the dye of lamp-black oil; its proximate cause is seeing enjoyment in things that fetter. Craving, growing as a river, is to be regarded as a fast-flowing river carrying one to the sea, taking one to the states of loss. Delusion (moha) has as its mark blindness of consciousness or lack of knowledge; as function, non-penetration or concealing the nature of the object; as manifestation, wrong practice or darkness; as proximate cause, unwise attention; it is the root of all that is unwholesome.

paraphrase: Wrong view (micchādiṭṭhi) is that by which one sees wrongly, or which sees wrongly, or mere wrong seeing: its mark is unwise insistence; its function is clinging; its manifestation is wrong adherence; its proximate cause is the wish not to see the noble ones and the like; it is to be regarded as the most blameworthy. Restlessness (uddhacca) is agitated state: its mark is non-calming; its function is unsteadiness, like water stirred by wind; its manifestation is bewilderment, like a flag fluttering in the wind or like ashes thrown up by a blow on a stone; its proximate cause is unwise attention to the non-calming of the mind; it is to be regarded as distraction of consciousness. The other factors are as stated for the unwholesome. The second unwholesome consciousness is like the first, but prompted and with sloth-torpor indeterminate. Sloth (thīna) is the sinking, torpor (middha) the drowsing: sloth has as its mark lack of energy and as function dispelling energy, as manifestation sinking; torpor has as mark unworkableness, as function smothering, as manifestation drooping or drowsy sleep; for both the proximate cause is unwise attention to discontent, lazy stretching and the like. Conceit (māna), indeterminate in the third and fourth, has as mark haughtiness, as function self-promotion, as manifestation vain-glory, as proximate cause greed dissociated from view; it is to be regarded as madness. The fifth to eighth are given in the same manner without wrong view or with joy left out.

paraphrase: In the two hate-rooted consciousnesses, the first has eleven fixed factors (contact, volition, applied thought, sustained thought, energy, life faculty, concentration, shamelessness, fearlessness of wrongdoing, hate, delusion), four "whatever" factors, and three indeterminate (envy, avarice, remorse), eighteen in all. Hate (dosa) is that by which one hates or which hates or mere hating: its mark is ferocity, like a struck snake; its function is to spread, like a fall of poison, or to burn its own support, like a forest fire; its manifestation is fury, like a foe who has found his chance; its proximate cause is the grounds of resentment; it is to be regarded as urine mixed with poison. Envy (issā) is envying: its mark is jealousy of others' success; its function is dissatisfaction with it; its manifestation is turning away from it; its proximate cause is others' success; it is to be regarded as a fetter. Avarice (macchariya) is the state of the miser: its mark is hiding one's own success, gained or to be gained; its function is not bearing to share it with others; its manifestation is shrinking or a bitter mood; its proximate cause is one's own success; it is to be regarded as an ugly state of mind. Remorse (kukkucca) is the state of having done wrong: its mark is later regret; its function is sorrow over what has been done and not done; its manifestation is remorse; its proximate cause is what has been done and not done; it is to be regarded as slavery.

paraphrase: The delusion-rooted consciousnesses. With doubt: the eleven are contact, volition, applied thought, sustained thought, energy, life faculty, consciousness-steadiness (cittaṭṭhiti), shamelessness, fearlessness of wrongdoing, delusion and doubt, plus restlessness and attention, thirteen. "Consciousness-steadiness" is weak concentration: only the steadiness of occurrence. Doubt (vicikicchā) is the absence of cure: its mark is uncertainty; its function is wavering; its manifestation is indecision or taking hold of no one side; its proximate cause is unwise attention; it is to be regarded as an obstacle to practice. With restlessness, the factors are those of the doubt-consciousness without doubt, twelve; since doubt is absent, resolve arises, and with it thirteen and concentration is stronger. Then, among the indeterminate, the resultant consciousnesses are of two kinds, root-less and with roots. In the root-less, eye-consciousness resultant on the wholesome or unwholesome has four factors in their own form (contact, volition, life faculty, consciousness-steadiness) and one "whatever" (attention), five; ear, nose, tongue and body consciousness are the same; the mind-element has these plus applied thought, sustained thought and resolve, eight. The rooted resultants in the sense sphere are like the eight wholesome sense-sphere ones, except that compassion and gladness (among the indeterminate) are absent in resultants, since resultants of the sense sphere have a single limited object.

paraphrase: On the fourfold clinging (upādāna) in the dependent-origination treatment of "feeling as condition for craving": clinging to sensual pleasures (kāmūpādāna), clinging to views (diṭṭhūpādāna), clinging to rites and observances (sīlabbatūpādāna) and clinging to a doctrine of self (attavādūpādāna). Their meanings: the first clings to sensual objects, or is itself sense-desire and clinging; "clinging" (upādāna) is firm grasping, the prefix upa- meaning firm as in upāyāsa; view is itself clinging, or clings to a view (as in "the self and the world are eternal", where a later view clings to an earlier); rites and observances (such as cow-virtue, cow-duty) are clinging in that one adheres to them as "purity thus"; clinging to a doctrine of self is clinging by which they say or take "self". The Dhammasaṅgaṇī's summary is quoted: clinging to sensual pleasures is "in sensual pleasures, sense-desire, sensual lust, sensual delight, craving, sensual affection, fever, swoon, fixation"; in short, the firmness of craving, the later craving grown firm through the earlier as strong support. Some say craving is the stretching out toward an object not yet reached, like a thief's hand groping in the dark, and clinging is the taking of the object reached, like grasping the goods; contentment with little is their opposite. The other three clingings are, in brief, just views; in detail, the firmness of the hundred and eight kinds of craving is clinging to sensual pleasures; the tenfold wrong view is clinging to views; the wrong grasp that purity comes from rites and observances is clinging to rites and observances (quotation given on p. 570).

paraphrase: Continuation. Clinging to rites and observances is quoted as the view "purity by virtue, by observance, by virtue-and-observance"; clinging to a doctrine of self is the twenty-fold view of a personal existence (sakkāyadiṭṭhi): "here the uninstructed ordinary person regards form as self" and so on. This is the summary of the states. On order: the order is threefold: of arising, of abandoning and of teaching. Since in a beginningless round there is no first arising of the defilements, the order of arising is not strictly stated, but in a manner of speaking, in one existence the clinging to a doctrine of self comes first, then adherence to eternalism or annihilationism: one who grasps "the self is eternal" takes up rites and observances for the purity of the self; one who grasps "it is annihilated", indifferent to another world, takes up sense pleasures; then views, rites and sense pleasures. In the order of abandoning, clinging to views and the rest are abandoned first, being to be cut by the stream-entry path, and clinging to sensual pleasures last, being to be cut by the arahat path. In the order of teaching, sense pleasures are taught first for their wide scope and evidence; then views; and of these two, rites and observances (coarse, seen in the behaviour of cows and dogs) before the doctrine of self (subtle).

paraphrase: The formations appear as ever new and short-lived, like a dewdrop at sunrise, a bubble on water, a line drawn on water, a mustard seed on an awl-tip, a flash of lightning, and as insubstantial and empty like illusion, mirage, dream, fire-wheel, city of spirits, foam and plantain. At this point the meditator has reached the knowledge of arising and passing away, the young insight. The ten imperfections of insight (vipassanūpakkilesa) now arise for one who has begun insight with this young insight; they do not arise in a noble disciple who has penetrated, nor in one who has wrongly practised, given up the subject or is lazy; they arise in a clansman who practises rightly and is earnest. They are: illumination (obhāsa), knowledge (ñāṇa), rapture (pīti), tranquillity (passaddhi), happiness (sukha), resolve (adhimokkha), exertion (paggaha), establishment of mindfulness (upaṭṭhāna), equanimity (upekkhā) and delight (nikanti). The text quotes: "how is the mind seized by restlessness about the Dhamma? For one attending to impermanence, illumination arises; he adverts to it as 'illumination is the Dhamma'; then comes distraction, restlessness; by that restlessness the mind is seized, and he does not know as it is the establishment (of the states) as impermanent, as suffering, as not self." Likewise with knowledge, rapture and the rest, up to delight.

paraphrase: When one of these arises the meditator thinks "such knowledge, such rapture, tranquillity, happiness, resolve, exertion, establishment, equanimity, delight has never arisen in me before; surely I have reached the path, reached the fruit", and takes what is not the path to be the path and what is not the fruit to be the fruit. For one who so takes it, the course of insight is lost (ukkantā); he sets aside his own basic subject and sits savouring the delight. The illumination and the rest are called imperfections because they are grounds (vatthu) of imperfection, not because they are unwholesome; delight is both an imperfection and a ground of imperfection. They are ten by ground and thirty by grasp: taking "my illumination has arisen" is grasping by view; "agreeable illumination has arisen" grasping by conceit; savouring it grasping by craving; so for each of the ten. Through them an unskilled, undiscerning meditator wavers and is distracted, regarding each as "this is mine, this I am, this is my self". The ancients say the mind trembles at illumination, knowledge, rapture, tranquillity, happiness, resolve, exertion, establishment, equanimity-and-adverting, and delight. The skilful, wise, discerning meditator, when they arise, thinks: "this illumination has arisen in me; but it is impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, of a nature to end, to pass, to fade, to cease"; or, "if illumination were the self, it would be right to take it as self; but taken as self, it is not-self, since it is not under control, impermanent because it is not after having been, and suffering since it is oppressed by arising and passing", as is set out in the seven-fold contemplation.

paraphrase: Concluding the imperfections: he regards illumination, knowledge and the rest as "this is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self", and so regarding does not waver or tremble at them. The ancients say: one whose understanding is practised in these ten spots is skilled in restlessness about the Dhamma and is not distracted. So not distracted, he unpicks the thirty-fold tangle of imperfections and defines the path and the not-path: illumination and the rest are not the path; the insight-knowledge that has entered the true course, free of imperfections, is the path. The knowledge that stands, knowing the path and the not-path, is the purification by knowledge and vision of what is path and not-path. At this point he has defined the three truths: by defining mind-and-matter in the purification of view he has defined suffering; by discerning conditions in the purification by overcoming doubt, the origin; by determining the right path here, the path. The chapter ends with the colophon, the twentieth chapter.

paraphrase: At the moment of the arahat path he emerges from the remaining fetters and latent tendencies (from lust for fine-material and immaterial existence, conceit, restlessness, ignorance; the latent conceit, latent lust for existence, latent ignorance), from the defilements that follow them and the aggregates, and outwardly from all signs: as quoted, "understanding in the turning away by emerging in both ways is knowledge in the path". In the development of the eight worldly attainments calm is stronger; in developing the contemplation of impermanence and so on, insight is stronger; in the moment of the noble path they occur yoked together, neither exceeding the other; so in the four knowledges of the paths there is a joining of both powers. The text quotes the Paṭisambhidā: for one emerging from the defilements accompanied by restlessness and from the aggregates, one-pointedness of mind, non-distraction, is concentration whose domain is cessation; for one emerging from the defilements accompanied by ignorance, insight in the sense of contemplation has cessation as domain; thus in the sense of emerging calm and insight are of one taste, yoked and not exceeding each other. Then, under "what is to be abandoned by which, and the abandoning", the text begins: in these four knowledges one should know what states are to be abandoned by each knowledge, states that come as fetters, defilements, wrongnesses, worldly conditions, avarice, perversions, ties, wrong courses, taints, floods, yokes, hindrances, adherences, clingings, latent tendencies, stains, unwholesome courses of action and unwholesome thoughts. Fetters are ten things that bind beings to aggregates, to the fruit of kamma and to suffering; of them five are higher fetters (lust for fine-material existence, for immaterial existence, conceit, restlessness, ignorance) (continued on p. 683).

paraphrase: The five lower fetters are personality view (sakkāyadiṭṭhi), doubt (vicikicchā), adherence to rites and observances, sensual lust and ill will (paṭigha), which bind to lower aggregates and the like. Defilements (kilesa), being themselves defiled and defiling their associated states, are ten: greed, hate, delusion, conceit, view, doubt, sloth, restlessness, shamelessness and fearlessness of wrongdoing. Wrongnesses (micchatta) are eight: wrong view, wrong intention, wrong speech, wrong action, wrong livelihood, wrong effort, wrong mindfulness and wrong concentration, or ten with wrong release and wrong knowledge. Worldly conditions (lokadhamma) are eight: gain and loss, fame and disrepute, pleasure and pain, blame and praise; here the text says liking for what is gained and resentment for what is not gained are taken under those. Avarice (macchariya) is fivefold: over dwelling, family, gain, teaching and praise. Perversions (vipallāsa) are three: of perception, of mind and of view, taking the impermanent, painful, not-self and unlovely as permanent, pleasant, self and beautiful. Ties (gantha) are four: covetousness, ill will, adherence to rites and observances, and the insistence that "this alone is truth". Wrong courses (agati) are doing what should not be done and not doing what should be done through desire, hate, delusion and fear. Taints (āsava) is a name for sensual lust, lust for existence, wrong view and ignorance, so called because they flow out (as far as change-of-lineage and the top of existence by way of object, or through the unguarded doors like water through the holes of a jar, in the sense of constant trickling), or because they make the suffering of the round flow (continued on p. 684).

paraphrase: Floods (ogha) are so called because they drag one into the ocean of existence and are hard to cross; yokes (yoga) because they give no release from the object and from suffering. Hindrances (nīvaraṇa) are the five, beginning with sensual desire, by way of covering, hindering and concealing consciousness. Adherence (parāmāsa) is wrong view, since it goes beyond the true nature of each thing and touches on what is untrue. Clingings (upādāna) are the four (sensual pleasures and the rest) as given in the dependent-origination treatment. Latent tendencies (anusaya) are seven, beginning with latent sensual lust, because being strong they lie latent, giving rise repeatedly to lust and the rest. Stains (mala) are three (greed, hate, delusion), being impure themselves and making others impure. Unwholesome courses of action are ten: killing, taking what is not given, misconduct in sensual pleasures, lying, slander, harsh speech, idle talk, covetousness, ill will and wrong view. Unwholesome thoughts are twelve (eight rooted in greed, two in hate, two in delusion). Which knowledge abandons what: the five fetters of personality view, doubt, adherence to rites, and lust and hate that lead to states of loss are to be cut by the first path knowledge; the rest of lust and hate, gross ones, by the second; subtle ones by the third; the five (lust for fine-material existence and the rest) by the fourth. Among defilements, view and doubt are cut by the first, hate by the third; greed, delusion, conceit, sloth, restlessness, shamelessness and fearlessness of wrongdoing by the fourth.

paraphrase: Abandoning by substitution of opposites (tad-aṅga-pahāna): abandoning of each state to be abandoned by a factor of knowledge that is its opposite. So defining mentality-materiality abandons personality view; discerning conditions abandons the view of no cause or wrong cause and the stain of doubt; comprehension in groups abandons the grasp of "I" and "mine" as a whole; determining path and not-path abandons the perception of the path in what is not the path; seeing arising abandons the annihilation view; seeing passing abandons the eternity view; appearance as fearful abandons the perception of no danger; seeing danger abandons the perception of enjoyment; contemplation of disenchantment abandons delight; desire for deliverance abandons non-desire for deliverance; reflection abandons non-reflection; equanimity abandons non-equanimity; conformity abandons the taking of the truth contrarily. Or, in the eighteen principal insights: contemplation of impermanence abandons the perception of permanence; of pain, the perception of pleasure; of not-self, the perception of self; of disenchantment, delight; of fading away, lust; of cessation, origin; of relinquishment, grasping; of destruction, the perception of compactness; of passing away, accumulating; of change, the perception of the stable; of the signless, the sign; of the desireless, the wish; of voidness, adherence; of insight into states that is higher understanding, adherence to substance; of knowledge and vision of things as they are, adherence through confusion; of danger, adherence to attachment; of reflection, non-reflection; of turning away, adherence through binding. Destruction contemplation, done by analysing away compactness, sees that impermanent and knows "destruction"; by it the perception of compactness is abandoned. Passing-away contemplation (vayānupassanā) is the resolve on cessation, seeing the breaking up of formations directly and by inference; by it accumulation is abandoned.
